clinicalPearls: Presents with unilateral, often severe, retro-orbital or periorbital pain accompanied by ipsilateral ophthalmoplegia
Caused by idiopathic granulomatous inflammation of the cavernous sinus or superior orbital fissure
Any combination of the third, fourth, and sixth cranial nerves may be involved, sometimes with the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve
Sympathetic fibres may be affected, producing a Horner syndrome, and optic nerve involvement can occur if the inflammation extends to the orbital apex
It is a diagnosis of exclusion, requiring careful ruling out of tumour, aneurysm, infection, and other inflammatory disease
MRI may show abnormal soft tissue in the cavernous sinus that enhances with contrast
The pain and ophthalmoplegia typically respond promptly to corticosteroids, and a dramatic response supports the diagnosis
reference.pathophysiology: Tolosa-Hunt syndrome is a non-specific granulomatous inflammation involving the cavernous sinus, superior orbital fissure, or orbital apex. The inflammatory tissue compresses and irritates the ocular motor nerves and the trigeminal fibres passing through this compartment, producing painful ophthalmoplegia. The cause is unknown and the histology resembles that of idiopathic orbital inflammation. Because the same anatomical region can be affected by tumour, aneurysm, infection, and systemic granulomatous disease, the syndrome remains a diagnosis of exclusion supported by imaging and steroid responsiveness.
additionalDifferentials: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma with skull base extension
Orbital apex fungal infection such as mucormycosis
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain and orbits with contrast focused on the cavernous sinus
Magnetic resonance or CT angiography to exclude an aneurysm
Inflammatory markers including erythrocyte sedimentation rate
Screening for systemic granulomatous disease such as sarcoidosis and vasculitis
Blood glucose to consider a diabetic nerve palsy
Biopsy in atypical or steroid-unresponsive cases
redFlags: Failure to respond to corticosteroids prompting reconsideration of tumour or infection
Signs of orbital apex involvement with visual loss
Features suggesting an aneurysm or invasive infection
Systemic symptoms pointing to malignancy or vasculitis
reference.prognosis: The syndrome usually responds well to corticosteroids with resolution of pain and gradual recovery of ophthalmoplegia, but recurrences are common and some patients retain residual nerve deficits.
pitfalls: Accepting the diagnosis without adequately excluding tumour, aneurysm, and infection
Interpreting any improvement on steroids as confirmation, since some tumours and lymphoma also respond transiently
Missing orbital apex extension threatening vision
Overlooking invasive fungal infection in an immunocompromised or diabetic patient
references: International Classification of Headache Disorders criteria
management: Systemic corticosteroids are the mainstay, typically producing rapid relief of pain and gradual recovery of the ophthalmoplegia
Confirm exclusion of tumour, aneurysm, infection, and systemic granulomatous disease before attributing symptoms and committing to immunosuppression
Analgesia for the severe retro-orbital pain during the acute phase
Slow corticosteroid taper guided by symptoms to reduce the risk of relapse
Steroid-sparing immunosuppression such as azathioprine or methotrexate for recurrent or corticosteroid-dependent disease
Serial clinical review and contrast MRI surveillance to confirm resolution of cavernous sinus inflammation and detect relapse
Refer to neurology and ophthalmology, with neurosurgical or biopsy input for atypical or treatment-resistant cases
